Q60755927.summary: Christ stands full-length and frontal, blessing with his right hand and holding a jewelled Gospel book, while the twelve apostles appear as busts, six in a column on each side, all turned toward him. With his large eyes fixed on the viewer and lips slightly parted, he seems about to send them out to preach the Gospel to the world. The plaque probably formed the centrepiece of a precious book cover, much like the book Christ himself carries.
facts: The Cleveland Museum of Art dates the plaque c. 970–980 and attributes it to Ottonian Milan.
Wikipedia notes that it is thought to come from the same workshop as the Magdeburg ivories, though it was probably always intended for a book binding.
Q60755927.notes: CMA 1967.65; 18.2 × 9.9 cm. Cleveland's culture string ('Ottonian, Italy, Milan, Gothic period, 10th century') contains an evident error ('Gothic'); place simplified to Milan.

cur:monumental-san-saba-healing-paralyti.summary: Under a tiled roof supported by columns, the paralysed man on his bed is lowered on ropes into the room, while in the foreground Christ, haloed and in a dark robe, stands among the people; at the right the healed man walks away with his bed on his back. Two moments of the Gospel story are thus shown together, with Greek inscriptions above.
facts: The fragment comes from the earlier oratory discovered beneath the nave of the 12th-century basilica of San Saba during excavations in May 1900.
The religious community here goes back to about 645, when monks who had fled the monastery of Saint Sabas (Mar Saba) in Palestine settled on the Little Aventine after attending the Lateran Council.

wga:zearly/2/2paintin/2mustair3.summary: In this red-ochre fresco, Christ, haloed and robed, steps forward and reaches out his hand to the mouth of a man who bows low before him, while apostles stand behind Christ and a group of onlookers watch from beneath an arch at the right. Though faded, the broad, rhythmic figures convey the moment of touch by which the silent man is healed. The scene belongs to the extensive Carolingian cycle of the life of Christ in the remote Alpine church of Müstair.
facts: The convent church of Saint John at Müstair, founded around 780 perhaps at Charlemagne's instigation, preserves the best-surviving cycle of Carolingian wall painting; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
The paintings were rediscovered in 1896 and fully uncovered by 1950; parts had been painted over in the 12th century.
The Web Gallery of Art places this scene on the north wall and suggests the painters were itinerant artists trained in a Byzantine-influenced Italian tradition.
wga:zearly/2/2paintin/2mustair3.notes: Title from the WGA. The specific miracle (deaf-mute of Mark 7 or the mute demoniac of Matthew 9:32–33) is not confirmed by a second source; Mark 7 is suggested because Christ touches the man's mouth. Müstair is in Switzerland, not Italy.
